claims.claim_text: The DSA's 2016 strategy account characterizes neoliberal political mobilization beginning in the 1970s in the United States and non-Communist Europe as seeking to severely weaken democratic decision-making in workplaces and elections.

Neoliberal reforms beginning in the 1970s in the United States and non-Communist Europe enabled corporations to evade virtually all accountability to their workers and the communities where they operated.
By the early 2000s, the post-World War II gains in working-class strength and security across the United States and non-Communist Europe had been substantially reversed.
In countries such as the United States, post-World War II gains were distributed in racialized and gendered ways.
The DSA's 2016 strategy account assesses the roughly thirty years after World War II as the twentieth century's high point of working-class strength and security.

In the U.S. welfare context described by the DSA's 2016 neoliberalism account, white people constituted the largest group of welfare beneficiaries despite racialized portrayals of African American and Latino recipients as subsidized by white taxpayers.
